# Adventures in Weight-Space Programming with Beaker

Last week, Sparks of Weight-Space Programming by Takehi et al. at MIT CSAIL caught our eye: it had one language model improve another by editing its weights directly, with no training run and no gradients. If such a mechanism were to hold up, a model could fix another model the way it already fixes a prompt or code, which is a step toward continual learning driven by models themselves.

Its headline result: GPT-6 Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B, a small model that runs out of thinking tokens on 93% of MATH-500 problems, mostly mid-loop, and lifted its accuracy from 7.9% to 48.1%.

We gave the same task to Beaker , our autonomous agent improver.

In about an hour, Beaker found a one-neuron edit that cuts loops and raises accuracy by 30 points. Qwen3.5-0.8B gets most math problems wrong because it hits its token limit before giving an answer, usually while stuck repeating lines that start with "Wait". Beaker traced the loops to a single neuron using only the weights and the scored answers of its edits, without running the model. Doubling that neuron's output lifted MATH-500 accuracy from 7.4% to 37.4%. When we analyzed the changes, we found that the neuron Beaker identified lowers the probability that the model writes "Wait". By doubling its output, Beaker reduced that probability further, allowing the model to get out of loops more often.

What else Beaker found:

- Its fix adds to Takehi et al.'s. Their larger edit doesn't stop the loops; it helps the model get out of them. So the two combine: Beaker's neuron edit on top of theirs reaches 58.8% on MATH-500, against 51.1% for their edit alone.

- Give Beaker a goal and a way to score it, and it edits the weights toward it, up to a point. It made answers shorter by default, but couldn't teach the model to say "I don't know".

- A cheaper model does about as well inside Beaker. With GPT-6.1 Sol, Beaker found and fixed the same neuron as with GPT-6 Astra and scored about as well on math: 37.4% against Astra's 38.6% without running the model, and 39.5% against 34.8% with model reads. It did so at a fraction of the cost: $4–16 per run, against $28–79.

## Weight-space programming, briefly

The idea is simple: instead of training a network, a language model reads its weights and writes new values directly. 1

Takehi et al. gave GPT-6 Astra a CPU Python session with the weights and a budget of GPU passes. Each pass runs the model once on a batch Astra picks: it can either generate answers with Astra's current edit, or run texts through the model to read its activations. We call this access reads + generation. Two experiments set the scene for ours:

- Breakout from zero weights: Astra wrote a small policy network for MinAtar Breakout that scored about 517 in one shot.

- Qwen math: with 10 or 25 passes, Astra's edits barely moved MATH-500 (12.3% and 14.1%). With 50, its best edit reached 48.1% by changing 64 output columns in each of layers 15 and 19.

In this post we investigate four questions:

- Can Beaker find such edits on its own, even without ever running the model?

- What do the edits change in the model's answers?

- Is something simpler as effective? 2

- Does the recipe work beyond fixing loops, for changing model behavior for example? 3

## Weight edits with Beaker

Beaker autonomously runs experiments to improve agents. It works in rounds: Beaker suggests a change, scores it on training cases (labeled examples with known answers), and keeps it only if the gain beats measured noise, repeating until it stops finding measurable improvements. The final result is reported on held-out cases Beaker never sees. For these experiments, Beaker edits the model's weights ( Figure 1 ).

We ran Beaker two ways:

- Without running the model. Beaker's harness runs GPT-6 Astra or GPT-6.1 Sol in a sandbox. It reads the weights and writes each edit as text files of new values for specific columns or rows of a tensor. It never runs the model itself. Its feedback is what the harness returns when it scores an edit (see below): for every training answer, the score, the final answer, its length, whether it finished, and the start and end of its thinking. That is stricter than Takehi et al.'s reads + generation, which let Astra run the model on prompts of its choice.

- With model reads. We connected a GPU service to Beaker's harness so Beaker can also ask for 25 reads per run: the model reads texts Beaker chooses and returns its activations and token probabilities, without generating anything. Beaker can also fetch the full text of answers the harness already generated, not just their start and end. It still can't have the model answer problems on demand: new answers come only when the harness scores an edit, as in the first setup. So this setup has the reads of Takehi et al.'s passes, but not the generation.

In both, Beaker builds a checkpoint for every edit, scores it on 256 training cases (128 GSM8K, 128 MATH) and keeps it only if it beats measured noise. MATH-500 is held out and run with Takehi et al.'s settings. 4

Reproduction. The unedited model scored 6.2–8.4% across our runs, against their 7.9%. Their edit, rebuilt bit for bit from its published diff , scored 51.1% in our harness against their 48.1%. All numbers below are ours except Takehi et al.'s 25-pass result (14.1%).

### Results at a glance

- Without running the model, Sol's best run reached 37.4% with a single edit, neuron 573 ×2, found in its first hour (the run lasted about 4 hours), and Astra reached 38.6% in about 5 hours with edits to five neurons, neuron 573 among them. Both runs had instructions that gave more hints than Takehi et al.'s prompt.

- With 25 model reads each, Sol reached 39.5% and Astra 34.8%.

Neuron numbers count the neurons of one layer's MLP, and neurons with no layer named are in layer 22. "×2" means a neuron's output column was doubled, and "+ gate" or "− gate" means a copy of its gate row, as long as its up row, was added to or subtracted from its up row, so the neuron's output grows faster as its gate opens. Four of these five runs found neuron 573.

Combined, Beaker's edits reach 43.0%. Between them, these runs found nine different neuron edits. Applied together, they lift MATH-500 from 8.2% to 43.0%, against 36.6% for neuron 573 ×2 alone in the same harness. Where runs edited the same neuron (neuron 573 in four runs, neuron 387 in two), we kept the edit from the best run:

- Layer 15: neuron 349 ×4

- Layer 18: neuron 1261 ×0.5

- Layer 22: neuron 573 ×2, neuron 387 ×2, neuron 2388 + gate

- Layer 23: neurons 613 and 1681 − gate, neurons 970 and 1004 with new output columns

The extra gain over neuron 573 alone comes from fewer answers cut off at the token limit (50%, against 62%). The answers that do finish are right a little less often (85%, against 93%). Interestingly, neuron 573 alone accounts for about four-fifths of the combined gain over the unedited model's 8.2%, which warrants a closer look at the role it plays and how Beaker identified it.

## Inside the one-neuron fix

To better understand what neuron 573 does, let's start by looking at how a layer contributes to the model's output.

At each position in the text, Qwen3.5-0.8B carries one vector of 1,024 numbers, the residual stream. 5 The token's row of the embedding matrix starts it off. Each of the 24 layers reads the vector and adds its own output to it. Only attention moves information between positions; the MLP works on each position's vector on its own. At the top, after a final norm, the model scores every token in its vocabulary by a dot product with each position's vector, and the highest scores are the likeliest tokens to come after that position.

- Each layer has a SwiGLU MLP of 3,584 neurons. Each neuron checks the stream for one pattern, using its row of the gate matrix W gate , which decides when it fires, and its row of the up matrix W up , which sets the size and sign of its activation.

- When the pattern is there, the neuron fires. It adds its output column, its column of the down matrix W down : a fixed list of 1,024 numbers, scaled by how strongly it fires. 6

- Editing a neuron's output column changes what it adds, every time it fires.

The edit our runs found doubles the output column of neuron 573 in layer 22's MLP ( Figure 3 ): 1,024 numbers, about a millionth of the model. In the formula above that is Δ w = w 573 , so the neuron's push doubles wherever it fires (the close-up in Figure 3 ). Just before "Wait", neuron 573 fires negative. Its column points toward "Wait", as we show from the weights below ( Figure 4 ), so the layer subtracts it: that lowers the stream's dot product with "Wait", the score the output layer uses, and makes "Wait" less likely. Takehi et al.'s edit, covered below, changes 64 columns per layer instead of one.

Each neuron fires with some strength.

Beaker found neuron 573 with both models. The first run to find it, with Sol, never ran the model. It started from the scored answers: every failed answer had run out of tokens mid-thought, and most were stuck repeating lines that restart with "Wait". So it searched the weights for neurons that control "Wait".

The weights alone are enough for that search because Qwen3.5 uses weight tying. The embedding table, a 248,320 × 1,024 matrix with one row per token, does two jobs: the first is to turn each input token into the starting value of its position's stream, the second is to score every possible next token. For the second, the model multiplies the table by the final stream at a position (after the final norm): each token's score is the dot product of its row with that stream, and a softmax turns the 248,320 scores into next-token probabilities. So the " Wait" row plays both parts. Wherever the input token is " Wait", the stream at that position starts as this row, and the score of " Wait" as the next token is this row's dot product with the final stream. This means you can read a neuron's effect on "Wait" directly from the weights: the more its output column points along the " Wait" row, the more its firing moves the score of "Wait".

For every MLP neuron in all 24 layers, Beaker measured how closely its output column points along tokens like " Wait", "Therefore" and </think> . Neuron 573 in layer 22 stood out, and its gate and up rows line up with " Wait" too ( Figure 4 ). Beaker read this as a built-in brake on "Wait" and doubled the column once, without trying other strengths. Its score on the 256 training cases went from 10.5% to 46.1%.

Weakening the column floods the thinking with "Wait" and accuracy collapses below 2%. Doubling it removes "Wait" and lifts accuracy to 36.6%; stronger multipliers plateau ( Figure 5 ).

A plain token ban does the same job. To ban a token, we lower its score before each token is sampled: for t = " Wait" (with a leading space) and t = "Wait", the logit ℓ t becomes ℓ t − 100 . After the softmax, that token's probability drops to at most e − 100 times what it was, so it is never sampled, and the other tokens split its share in proportion to their own probabilities.
